author: A. Y. Campbell
title: Nevada faces shortage of physical therapists, experts discuss solutions on Brewing Better Health
text:
Nevada’s shortage of physical therapists and its impact on public health were discussed in the latest episode of Brewing Better Health, released June 10. Daryl Lawson, professor and director of the Doctorate of Physical Therapy Program at the University of Nevada, Reno School of Public Health, joined Dean Muge Akpinar-Elci to address issues surrounding pain management, prevention, and access to care.
Lawson said that Nevada ranks third from the bottom in physical therapists per 100,000 residents and noted that this gap is even wider outside major metropolitan areas like Reno-Sparks and Las Vegas. He emphasized a broader approach to patient care: “If you really look and listen, it could be more of a public health issue. Maybe transportation is the reason they can’t get there. Maybe it’s their housing, maybe it’s their diet or food. There could be so many other things why this person that walks into your clinic is not getting better.”
The new Doctorate of Physical Therapy Program at the University is housed within the School of Public Health with an aim to train students to think about population-level health needs as well as individual ones. Lawson said, “Here we look broader… which is really exciting, so we can make an impact on our state.” The program also focuses on recruiting students from Northern Nevada communities with hopes they will serve those same communities after graduation.
Lawson has also developed sensor-based technology for monitoring patients with diabetic foot ulcers remotely. This innovation aims to help patients who have difficulty attending frequent appointments due to transportation or cost barriers by allowing them daily treatment at home while clinicians monitor progress remotely.
Discussing misconceptions in physical therapy regarding pain management, Lawson said, “It’s a misconception if you don’t recognize all those types of things and, on a bigger scale, try to help with those things.” He advised listeners that understanding where pain comes from is essential before learning how best to manage it for quality-of-life improvements.
Lawson concluded by emphasizing interdisciplinary connection as key for advancing public health efforts: “That is public health in a nutshell to me… What gives me hope is being with the School of Public Health.” Brewing Better Health brings together leaders and practitioners from across disciplines for conversations about how public health affects everyday life.
